blocks.text: ZECHARIAH SON OF JEHOIADA THE PRIEST, STONED IN THE COURT OF THE HOUSE OF THE LORD · TWO KINGDOMS
Zechariah. “The LORD look upon it, and require it.”
SCRIPTURE CALLS
Prophet
ERA
Two kingdoms 930–586 BC
IN THE DAYS OF
Joash
BOOK
None bears the name
HOW THE WORD CAME
“The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, which stood above the people”; he spoke with “Thus saith God”.

How the word came
“The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, which stood above the people”; he spoke with “Thus saith God”. 2 Chronicles 24:20
Just before, Chronicles says of the time after Jehoiada's death: “Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again unto the LORD”. 2 Chronicles 24:19

COMPANIONS AND OPPONENTS
Who stood with him, and against him
Jehoiada the priest, his father
HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
He was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD at the king's command, and as he died he said, “The LORD look upon it, and require it.” 2 Chronicles 24:21–22

Chronicles goes on: at the end of the year the Syrians came and “executed judgment against Joash”, and his own servants slew him on his bed “for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest”. It does not say here that this came according to Zechariah's word. 2 Chronicles 24:23–25

Jesus spoke of “the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar” (Matthew); Luke has “the blood of Zacharias, which perished between the altar and the temple”. Whether this is the same man is a question below. Matthew 23:35 Luke 11:51
TRADITION SAYS

The Rabbis said Zechariah was killed in the priests' court on a Sabbath that was also the Day of Atonement, and that when Nebuzar-adan came to destroy the Temple his blood “began to boil”; Nebuzar-adan killed many thousands to appease it, until he cried out to Zechariah and the blood was still.[53] Who says so: The Talmud (Gittin 57b; Sanhedrin 96b) and Lamentations Rabbah, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia, rabbinic writings; reported 1906
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
Yes; Jehoiada had a second name, or was the grandfather
Geneva notes (1599); Albert Barnes (1832); the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew (1880–1897), as possibilities

The Geneva note: “Of Joiada, who was also called Barach-jah”. Barnes notes that it was common to have two names. The Pulpit Commentary also allows that Barachiah was the father and Jehoiada the grandfather. Ellicott calls such suggestions “hypotheses invented for the occasion, without a shadow of evidence”. Matthew 23:35 2 Chronicles 24:20 [25][1][100][21]
Yes; “son of Barachias” is a slip or a later addition
Ellicott's commentary (c. 1878–1884); A. Carr (1878); H. A. W. Meyer (1879)

Luke 11:51 has no father's name, and Jerome reports that the Gospel of the Nazarenes read “son of Joiada” (Pulpit Commentary). Ellicott: “the mistake of a transcriber”; Carr: the words “are possibly interpolated”; Meyer: an error from confusing him with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). Carr and Meyer add that from Abel to this Zechariah runs from Genesis to Chronicles, the first and last books of the Hebrew canon. Luke 11:51 Zechariah 1:1 [21][8][76][100]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 3
2 Chronicles 24 Matthew 23 Luke 11
PASSAGES · 3
2 Chronicles 24:17–25 Matthew 23:35 Luke 11:51
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Chronicles does not call Zechariah a prophet in so many words; it says the Spirit of God came upon him, after saying the LORD “sent prophets to them”.
Chronicles places his death “in the court of the house of the LORD”; it does not say “between the temple and the altar”.
Kings does not tell Zechariah's death; it is in Chronicles only.
